subtitulo: Three past verbs carry a whole trip — sono andato, ho mangiato, mi è piaciuto
cena: Someone has asked what you did yesterday and every sentence you own is stuck in the present.
frasePiso: You do not need the past tense of the language. You need three verbs, and one of them is just a feeling.
decisao: contar o dia de ontem com três verbos no passado em vez de descrever tudo no presente e virar a pessoa que só responde sim

steps.pt: The moment you can say what you did yesterday, you stop being a person who orders things and start being someone with a trip.

steps.acao: This is the opening. Answer with where you went, not with a yes.
steps.pt: So, what did you do yesterday?
The frame is ho or sono, plus the verb. Sono andato — I went. Sono andata if you are a woman.

steps.promptPt: Say where you went yesterday. One place, one sentence. Speak now.

steps.pt: Verb two: ho mangiato. I ate. This one takes ho, not sono, and that difference is the whole grammar you need here.

steps.promptPt: Say what you ate. Name the dish, not the restaurant. Speak now.
steps.es: Ho mangiato la bistecca alla fiorentina.
steps.pinyin: oh man-JA-to la bis-TEK-ka AL-la fyo-ren-TEE-na
steps.tts: Ho mangiato la bistecca alla fiorentina.

steps.es: Ah, quella vera! E dove, scusa?
steps.pt: Ah, the real one! And where, may I ask?
steps.tts: Ah, quella vera! E dove, scusa?

steps.pt: Verb three is the one that keeps the conversation alive: mi è piaciuto. I liked it. Literally, it pleased me.

steps.promptPt: Say you liked it very much. Speak now.
String two of them together — where and what. Speak now.
steps.es: Sono andato al mercato e ho comprato del formaggio.
steps.pinyin: SO-no an-DA-to al mer-KA-to eh oh kom-PRA-to del for-MAJ-jo
steps.pt: I went to the market and bought some cheese.
steps.tts: Sono andato al mercato e ho comprato del formaggio.

steps.pt: Notice the shape of the frame: movement takes sono, doing-something-to-a-thing takes ho. That covers most of what you will say.

steps.promptPt: Say you walked a lot. Speak now.
Say what surprised you, so the story has a point. Speak now.
steps.pt: I wasn't expecting it to be so beautiful.

steps.acao: Do not just say yes. Name the one thing you would go back for.
steps.es: Eh, tutti dicono così. E domani dove andate?
steps.pt: Eh, everyone says that. And tomorrow, where are you going?
steps.tts: Eh, tutti dicono così. E domani dove andate?

steps.promptPt: Answer the tomorrow question and hand it back to them. Speak now.
steps.es: Domani andiamo a Siena. Lei c'è stato?
steps.pinyin: do-MA-nee an-DYA-mo a see-EH-na. lay cheh STA-to
steps.pt: Tomorrow we're going to Siena. Have you been?
steps.tts: Domani andiamo a Siena. Lei c'è stato?

steps.promptPt: Say the one thing you did not like, lightly. A trip with no low point sounds invented. Speak now.
steps.es: Il museo, invece, non mi è piaciuto tanto.
steps.pinyin: eel moo-ZEH-o, een-VE-che, non mee eh pya-CHOO-to TAN-to
steps.pt: The museum, though, I didn't like much.
steps.tts: Il museo, invece, non mi è piaciuto tanto.

steps.es: Ieri sono andato a Firenze. Ho mangiato la bistecca alla fiorentina. Mi è piaciuto moltissimo.
steps.pinyin: ee-EH-ri SO-no an-DA-to a fee-REN-tse. oh man-JA-to la bis-TEK-ka AL-la fyo-ren-TEE-na. mee eh pya-CHOO-to mol-TEES-see-mo
steps.pt: Shadow the three verbs in the order a story wants them.
steps.tts: Ieri sono andato a Firenze. Ho mangiato la bistecca alla fiorentina. Mi è piaciuto moltissimo.

steps.pt: I06 done. Sono andato, ho mangiato, mi è piaciuto — where, what, and how it landed. That is a story.

secoes.corpo: Verbs of movement and change take sono and their ending agrees with you: sono andato, sono andata, siamo andati. Verbs that do something to a thing take ho and never change: ho mangiato, ho visto, ho comprato. Getting this wrong is the most forgiven mistake in Italian.

secoes.titulo: Mi è piaciuto is backwards on purpose
secoes.corpo: It means it pleased me, so the thing is the subject. This is why it is è and not ho, and why it changes with the thing rather than with you: mi è piaciuta la città, mi sono piaciuti i musei.

secoes.titulo: A low point makes it true
secoes.corpo: Saying you liked everything reads as politeness rather than experience. Naming one thing that did not land — non mi è piaciuto tanto — is what turns a report into a conversation someone wants to continue.
Every account of your day should end with a question. Lei c'è stato? costs three words and moves the conversation from an interview to an exchange.

permissao: You are allowed to get sono and ho the wrong way round. Italians mix them up too in fast speech, nobody misunderstands you because of it, and the version of this part where you wait until you have the rule solid is the version where you never tell anyone about your day.
espelho: Anyone who has answered a friendly 'how was your day' with a flat 'good' because assembling the real answer felt like work knows the reflex this part is aimed at. It is not a grammar problem — it is the cost of assembling a sentence being higher than the reward, until it suddenly is not.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You tell someone you loved a famous town and they answer eh, tutti dicono così — everyone says that.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: They are dismissing what I said, or mocking the tourist for liking the obvious thing.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: It is a conversational move that asks for the next level of detail rather than closing the topic. Italian small talk tends to prod for specifics; agreeing blandly is what ends a conversation, not what continues it.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Answer with the specific: the dish, the street, the hour of the day. Then hand the question back.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get the real recommendation — the version they give people who said something concrete — instead of the one they give everybody.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not when the person is genuinely busy and the exchange is transactional; at a counter with a queue, the short warm answer is the correct one.
